questions.q: How does scalability differ from performance as an NFR category?
options: They are the same requirement, just measured with different tools
Performance is a Shield feature; scalability is a base-platform feature
Scalability only applies to Apex code, while performance only applies to declarative automation
Performance asks whether the system is fast enough right now; scalability asks whether it stays fast enough as data, users, and transactions grow
questions.explain: Performance evaluates current speed under current load. Scalability evaluates whether that speed holds up as volume grows over time — a system can score well on one and poorly on the other.

questions.q: Why should a scalability NFR separate data-volume, user-volume, and transaction-volume growth into distinct statements?
options: Because Salesforce licensing requires them to be tracked separately
Because they can grow independently of each other and stress different parts of the architecture, so a single blended statement gives the architect nothing specific to design against
Because only data-volume growth is ever relevant to a Salesforce architect
Because transaction-volume growth is always proportional to user-volume growth
questions.explain: A B2C org might see explosive data growth with flat user counts, while an acquisition could double user count with no change in data volume. Treating them as one undifferentiated 'must scale' requirement gives no concrete target to design against.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend expressing a scalability NFR as a growth curve (e.g., year one vs. year three volumes) rather than a single number?
options: Because Salesforce requires growth projections to be submitted annually
Because a single number is always more accurate than a trend line

Because the design that's adequate for the starting volume may not hold at a later volume, and a trajectory forces the architect to decide up front whether the design holds at the end state or only the start
Because growth curves are only relevant to transaction-volume scalability, not data-volume
questions.explain: A single number only describes a snapshot. A growth curve forces an explicit decision about whether the chosen design holds up at the projected end state, not just at today's volume, and gives future architects a documented basis for revisiting the decision.

questions.q: What is the primary intended use case for Salesforce Big Objects?
options: Storing very large volumes of data (hundreds of millions to billions of records), such as long-term archival or audit history, outside standard object query infrastructure
Replacing standard objects for all day-to-day transactional data entry
Encrypting sensitive fields at rest
Running real-time Apex triggers on high-frequency updates
questions.explain: Big Objects are designed for massive data volumes that need to be retained and occasionally queried but don't need the full standard-object feature set like triggers or most declarative automation — typically archival or long-term audit history.

questions.q: A list view against a 10-million-record custom object filters on a non-indexed text field and performs a full table scan. What scalability lever from this lesson most directly addresses this problem?
options: Switching the object to a Big Object
Moving all automation from synchronous to asynchronous Apex
Reducing the number of licensed users on the org
Designing the query or list view to filter on indexed fields, making it a selective query
questions.explain: An unselective query against a large object forces a full table scan regardless of other scaling work. Ensuring queries and list views filter on indexed fields (a selective query) is the most direct and common fix for this specific problem.
